answer.question: How do multicolumn indexes work in PostgreSQL?
answer.answer:
In PostgreSQL, you can define one index over several columns, e.g. `CREATE INDEX test2_mm_idx ON test2 (major, minor);` This suits queries like `WHERE major = constant AND minor = constant`. Only B-tree, GiST, GIN and BRIN support multiple key columns. An index can have up to 32 columns, including INCLUDE columns. The limit can be changed when building PostgreSQL.

How well it works depends on the index type:
- **B-tree:** It can be used with conditions on any subset of its columns, but it is most efficient when the leading (leftmost) columns are constrained. Equality constraints on leading columns, plus any inequality on the first column without an equality, limit the part of the index that is scanned. Constraints on columns further right are checked inside the index. This saves table visits but doesn't necessarily shrink the scan. If the skip scan optimization applies, it can reduce the portion read even when an earlier column has no equality constraint.
- **GiST:** It can be used with any subset of columns. The first column matters most for how much of the index is scanned. The index is relatively ineffective if the first column has few distinct values.
- **GIN:** It can be used with any subset of columns. Effectiveness is the same whichever columns the query uses.
- **BRIN:** It can be used with any subset of columns. Effectiveness is the same whichever columns the query uses. The only reason to use several BRIN indexes instead of one multicolumn index is to get a different pages_per_range setting.
